### p4
*2026-08-15 14:05*

> ok that's cool! so what is the "ask" input box currently wired up to?

No agent yet — it's wired to two dumb-but-honest mechanisms, one per half of "find or file":

**Find** is plain word matching, entirely on-device:
- Your query's words (minus little words like "my", "do") are matched against the **toolbar's tool labels** — a hit renders an "open ‹tool›" chip that sends the tool's own event and closes the panel, landing you in it.
- The same words are scored by overlap against the **feature tree's** names, purposes, and intro paragraphs (the `tree.json` the chooser already loads) — the top three render as ordinary chooser rows, so tap-to-read-the-intro and drill-to-the-page work unmodified. That's it: no model, no server round trip, just token overlap.

**File** is the real pipeline, and it goes all the way through:
- "Send to the builder" (or automatically, when nothing matched) sends an `Ask` event carrying your words and a timestamp. `ask.rs` appends `{t, text, status: "asked"}` to your user-scoped `asks` var, and `/scope` does what it does with all state: syncs it to your other devices and persists it on the mini at `/tmp/muon-vars/user.<you>.asks.json`.
- Two readers are wired to that file: **deploy** prints every ask still `"asked"` at the moment of shipping (beside its nodeless-release warning), and **me** — the dev-session agent reads the inbox at session start, per the doctrine's "agent on a delay" starting point.

So today the intelligence budget is: word overlap on the find side, and a human-latency agent (this session) on the build side. The named next rungs are the lifecycle states on the feature list (asked → proposed → in progress → awaiting update → shipped), where my proposal for an ask would be the prospective node's `## user` paragraph, approved before I build it. Nothing marks an ask as addressed yet either — status never leaves `"asked"` until that lifecycle arrives.

### p5
*2026-08-15 14:07*

> I wonder if this is a good time to talk about "minimal updates" - when there's only a small number of new features to ship, can we think of a more efficient way than upgrading the entire muon app? Like, just patching in the functions that changed?

Good timing — this touches doctrine (the feature is the unit, so it should be the unit of *update* too). Before I sketch the ladder, let me verify what an update actually costs today — especially whether the cache wipe takes the 130MB speech model with it:

Here's my assessment — filed in notes.md as a proposal.

**The surprise: "patch the changed functions" aims at the wrong bytes.** The entire composed client is ~220KB; the wasm alone is 130KB and rebuilds as one blob (Rust gives us no honest function-level patching, and at that size it isn't worth fighting for). What's actually expensive about an update is:

1. **Eviction is a sledgehammer.** The ritual deletes the whole `muon` cache, and the service worker puts *everything* in there — so the 133MB whisper model dies with the 85KB of HTML it was standing next to. Every update quietly re-buys the model on the next transcription.
2. **Every release reloads every client**, even a server-only fix where nothing a client runs has changed.

So the ladder, cheapest first:

**A. Artifact-aware updates** — my recommendation for the next rung. Deploy exports a `manifest.json` mapping each site file to a content hash. The apply ritual diffs the running manifest against the new one and evicts *only changed paths*. Consequences fall out immediately: the model survives every update; a server-only release becomes a version stamp with **no reload at all** (nothing in the client manifest changed); and a typical one-feature release re-fetches ~90KB of html + maybe the wasm. This rides the path-stamping we built this morning and is a small node plus a deploy tweak.

**B. Split composition** — emit per-feature fragment files instead of one composed index.html, so a changed feature invalidates only its own file. Real linker work for marginal gain at 85KB; parked until the app is big enough to feel it.

**C. Hot patching — and this is the doctrinally interesting one.** A "soft reload" (fetch new wasm, re-instantiate in place, carry the state over) is nearly buildable — seamless's stash already proved the state-carry half. But true patching of live JS features needs **re-linkable chains**: today each wrap captures `existing` in a closure, so you can't replace a link without rebuilding the whole chain. A chain *registry* with indirection would fix that — and that is exactly the mechanism runtime feature-ticks need too. The context manager (tick a feature off *without* a reload) and minimal updates converge on the same missing linker primitive. Build one, get the other nearly free.

My suggestion: do A now — it makes most updates effectively free and fixes the model-eviction bug as a side effect — and park C as the named research fork that the context manager will eventually cash in. Want me to build A?

> ## TL;DR: Agent SDK Requires API Key Billing, Cannot Use Max Subscription
> 
> **The short answer to all four questions is: Agent SDK strictly requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` with per-token API billing. It has no support for Claude Max subscription authentication or usage.**

> ---
> 
> ## Detailed Findings
> 
> ### 1. **Agent SDK Authentication: API Key Only**
> 
> The Agent SDK **does not support Claude Max subscription authentication**. It requires an API key from the Claude Console ([platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/)), set as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`:
> 
> ```bash
> export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-...
> ```
> 
> **Critical policy restriction** (from Agent SDK docs):
> &gt; "Unless previously approved, Anthropic does not allow third party developers to offer claude.ai login or rate limits for their products, including agents built on the Claude Agent SDK. Please use the API key authentication methods described in this document instead."
> 
> The Agent SDK supports three authentication methods, **none of which use subscription credentials**:
> - **API keys** (static) — created in Claude Console
> - **Workload Identity Federation** (WIF) — for cloud workloads (AWS/GCP/Azure/OIDC)
> - **Cloud provider credentials** (Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry) — set provider-specific env vars
> 
> There is no OAuth token flow for subscription usage, and `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` does not exist for Agent SDK; it only works with the Claude Code CLI interactive mode.
> 
> ---
> 
> ### 2. **Claude Code CLI Headless (`claude -p`) — Limited Subscription Support**
> 
> Running `claude -p` (non-interactive CLI) has **two modes**:
> 
> **Without `--bare` (interactive login allowed):**
> - Can use subscription login if you've authenticated via `claude setup` or the CLI
> - Reads OAuth credentials from the system keychain
> - **Permitted for one-off scripted tasks**, but unclear if repeated programmatic usage violates ToS
> 
> **With `--bare` (recommended for automation):**
> - Explicitly **does not use subscription login**
> - **Requires** `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env var
> - Starts faster; skips hooks, plugins, MCP servers, and auto-memory
> - **Recommended mode for scripted/CI use**
> 
> **Policy gap:** The docs do not explicitly address whether repeated `claude -p` automation on subscription usage (non-bare mode) is permitted. The safer assumption is **it is not supported for programmatic agent pipelines** — the policy quote above forbids offering subscription-backed programmatic access without prior approval.
> 
> ---
> 
> ### 3. **Setup for Agent SDK + Headless Mac Mini Server**
> 
> On a headless machine with no browser, use **bare mode with an API key**:
> 
> **Python SDK:**
> ```python
> import asyncio
> from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions
> 
> async def main():
>     async for message in query(
>         prompt="Find and fix the bug in auth.py",
>         options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
>             allowed_tools=["Read", "Edit", "Bash"],
>             permission_mode="acceptEdits"
>         )
>     ):
>         if message.type == "result":
>             print(f"Done: {message.subtype}")
> 
> asyncio.run(main())
> ```
> 
> Set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the environment:
> ```bash
> export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-...
> python agent.py
> ```
> 
> **TypeScript SDK:**
> ```bash
> npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk
> export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-...
> npx tsx agent.ts
> ```
> 
> **Headless CLI (if you prefer CLI over SDK):**
> ```bash
> export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-...
> claude --bare -p "Fix the bug in auth.py" --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash"
> ```
> 
> No browser or OAuth flow needed; the API key is sufficient.
> 
> ---
> 
> ### 4. **Billing Limits: Max x20 vs API Pay-Per-Token**
> 
> | Aspect | Claude Max x20 (Subscription) | Claude API (Agent SDK) |
> |--------|------|---------|
> | **Model** | claude.ai interactive use only | API access (agent SDK, scripts) |
> | **Billing** | Fixed monthly (~$20 USD) | Pay-per-token: $1–$50/MTok by model |
> | **Included usage** | Yes (e.g., "20x faster for 50M tokens/day") | No; billed à la carte |
> | **Rate limits** | claude.ai tier-based (not published) | API tier-based: Start → Build → Scale |
> | **Practical for hobby pipeline** | Not available for programmatic use | ~$0.50–$2 per 100 API calls (Haiku/Sonnet) |
> 
> **Example: 50 requests/day for 30 days at Haiku pricing:**
> - Input: 5k tokens/request × 50 = 250k tokens/day
> - Output: ~1k tokens/request × 50 = 50k tokens/day
> - Cost: (250M × $1 + 50M × $5) / 1M ÷ 30 days ≈ **$0.01–$0.10/day** (~$0.30–$3/month)
> 
> **Max subscription does not cover this—it's separate.** You need both subscriptions if you use both services (interactive + programmatic).
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Recommended Path for Your Use Case
> 
> Build your server-side agent pipeline with:
> 1. **API key created in [Claude Console](https://platform.claude.com/)**
> 2. **Agent SDK (TypeScript/Python)** with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env var
> 3. **Bare mode for `claude -p` calls** if you use the CLI
> 4. **No integration with Max subscription** — they are separate products
> 
> For a small hobby pipeline (dozens of requests/day), cost is negligible (~$1–$5/month). For production, request enterprise pricing from [sales@anthropic.com](mailto:sales@anthropic.com).

**Your subscription question — answered authoritatively (docs-verified):**
- **The Agent SDK cannot use your Max subscription.** It's API-key-only (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`), pay-per-token. The docs are explicit: *"Anthropic does not allow third party developers to offer claude.ai login or rate limits for their products, including agents built on the Claude Agent SDK."* So the "API keys as secrets per user" route means each user pays per-token — but at hobby scale that's genuinely tiny: a few dozen requests a day runs roughly **$1–5/month** on Sonnet, pennies on Haiku.
- **Headless `claude -p` under your subscription login does work** — I tested it live on this laptop: it answered on your Max login, no API key. That's fine for personal scripting, but the docs steer sustained programmatic pipelines toward `--bare` mode + API key; a multi-user muon backend riding your personal subscription would be exactly what the policy quote forbids.
- The mini already has the `claude` CLI installed (2.1.56) but isn't logged in — so it's ready for the API-key route whenever you mint a key (`~/.agent-config.json`, the Vonage pattern).

**The "type into this terminal" idea — done, without the keystroke hack.** Injecting keystrokes via AppleScript is possible but fragile (accessibility permissions, focus stealing, wrong window). The cleaner equivalent: **this session now watches the inbox itself.** I've armed a persistent monitor that polls the mini's ask store every 60 seconds over ssh — the moment an ask lands with status `"asked"`, it fires an event that wakes me, mid-conversation or idle. Type into the ask box on your phone and it effectively types into my terminal. That's the doctrine's "dev-session agent on a delay" made literal, with the delay at about a minute — and it runs on your subscription because it *is* just me, no new billing, no secrets.

**So the pipeline ladder now reads:**
1. **Live now:** ask box → mini → this session wakes → I run the five-step loop on it (place, node, implement, prove, ship) → the answer arrives as an awaiting update on your devices. The whole request lifecycle already has both ends built.
2. **When it should outlive my session:** API key on the mini + `claude --bare -p` (or the SDK) invoked per ask by a small watcher — same inbox, same file, just a different agent behind it. Per-user keys as secrets fits the fm scope model (a user-scoped secret is just a var that never syncs to devices).

Want to test it? File an ask from your phone — something small and real — and we'll see the full loop run: your words arrive here, become a node, and ship back to you as an update to review.

**The speedup is real.** Browser benchmarks put WebGPU at **10–15x over wasm** depending on model and hardware; Gemma-class models typically run 20–60 tok/s in-browser on GPU, and Xenova's recent demo hit 255 tok/s on an M4 (fun footnote: he had Fable 5 — this model — write the custom WebGPU kernels for it). **FunctionGemma on WebGPU: yes, today, on desktop.** Transformers.js v3 has a WebGPU backend and the official FunctionGemma demos run fully in-browser on it.

**On your iPhone: the GPU is willing, the runtime is the problem — and it just got worse than we knew.** The handover already carried the known bug (ort's jsep requests more limits than Safari grants; haze's `required_limits: adapter.limits()` recipe is the named fix, sitting in phone.md). But the search surfaced [onnxruntime issue #26827](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/issues/26827): on Safari/WebKit 26, jsep builds exhibit **400%+ CPU and 1–14GB memory that persists after inference completes**, eventually crashing — and it reproduces in webgpu *and* wasm modes of the jsep build. That's the very environment whisper's five hard-won facts came from. So "can we run FunctionGemma on webgpu on the phone" is currently gated not by Apple's WebGPU (iOS 26 ships it, and haze proves the GPU works fine from Rust/wgpu *on your actual phone*) but by ort-web's health on WebKit.

Escape routes, in order of cheapness:
1. **Track ort** — the limits fix plus #26827's resolution may arrive as a version pin bump; when it lands, it unlocks FunctionGemma *and* the ~5–10x whisper upgrade in one move (they ride the same runtime).
2. **The Rust-native path** — burn's wgpu backend runs in-browser, and muon is already Rust/wasm with proof (via haze) that wgpu works on target hardware. Muon owning its own inference runtime instead of riding ort would be very fm — real work, but it sidesteps Microsoft's WebKit bugs entirely.

So the strategy writes itself: **build the find rung now (no GPU needed, instant, 8MB), let the call rung wait on whichever of ort-repair or burn-wgpu matures first** — and either way that repair pays twice, because whisper is waiting on the same door.

> can't we just patch ort-web? is it not open-source?

It is open-source (MIT, microsoft/onnxruntime) — and muon is unusually well-positioned to patch it, because we don't even consume ort through a CDN or npm at runtime: `fetch_stt.py` pins the exact dist bytes into `phone/assets/stt/`, so whatever we patch stays patched, deterministically, under our own roof. Let me check one thing first — whether upstream has already fixed the limits bug since our pin:

No confirmed upstream fix — #26827 is still open. Let me look at our actual pinned bytes to see how patchable the limits request is:

It's MIT-licensed, we already self-host the exact pinned bytes — and it turns out we don't even need to fork it. Looking at what's actually inside our pin changed the plan for the better:

**What the pinned bundle revealed.** The `requiredLimits` in `ort.webgpu.bundle.min.mjs` isn't computed in JS — it's emscripten marshalling glue: the C++ side writes the limits it *wants* into wasm memory, the JS reads them out field by field (`maxStorageBufferBindingSize`, `maxBufferSize`, …) and passes them to `adapter.requestDevice()`. Safari grants less than ort asks for, `requestDevice` rejects, and that's our wasm fallback. Patching the minified marshalling code is possible but ugly — and there are *two* bundles with `requestDevice` calls (transformers.min.js carries its own).

**The cleaner move: don't patch ort at all — shim the platform.** `engine.js` is *our* file (the phone node owns it), and it runs before ort loads. Ten lines there can wrap `GPUAdapter.prototype.requestDevice` to clamp every requested limit to what the adapter actually offers — haze's `required_limits: adapter.limits()` recipe, applied globally, catching both bundles at once. No forked minified files, no re-patching on every `fetch_stt.py` re-pin, provenance lives in a proper feature node (the named refinement already waiting in phone.md). Clamping is safe in practice here: whisper-tiny's actual buffers are far below Safari's grants — it's the same GPU haze already drives happily.

**The honest caveat stays #26827.** The shim fixes the *door* (device creation); the WebKit-26 jsep pathology (runaway CPU/memory *after* inference) is a separate, undiagnosed illness. The shim is also exactly the instrument we need to find out whether it bites *our* workload: with webgpu unlocked we can watch CPU/memory on a real transcription via the diag channel and the sim. If it does bite, then yes — real ort surgery or an upstream wait, with burn-wgpu as the sovereign escape route.

So the experiment, when you want it run: shim node under `phone`, clear the `muonSttDevice` failure memo, sim first (the `say`→transcript rig), then your phone with diag watching for the #26827 signature. Upside if it works: ~5–10x on whisper immediately, and the FunctionGemma door opens on the same hinge. Say go and I'll build it.
